files.lesson.md: --- order: 10 unit: pythagoras node: AC9M8M06 n2 uses: [AC9M7N01 n3] # square roots between whole numbers title: Finding a side summary: "Pythagoras finds any side. For the hypotenuse, add the squares: c² = a² + b². For a shorter side, subtract from the hypotenuse's square: b² = c² − a². Then take the square root, and check the hypotenuse is still the longest." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Ladders, ramps and TV screens all hide a right-angled triangle, and sometimes the side you need is not the longest one." connection: ladder-1-in-4 # data/connections/maths.yml (pilot: opening situation and Make; documentation only) app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8285 url: http://127.0.0.1:8285/index.html readySelector: "#sl-b" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: tri.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Hypotenuse 10 and one side 6: the missing square is $100 - 36 = 64$, so the side is $\\sqrt{64} = 8$." } explainClip: query: { code: "@tri.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "A shorter side" say: "To find a shorter side, subtract." clip: - caption: { text: "We want c = 10 with a = 6. Which b?", say: "We want the long side to be ten. Which short side?" } - wait: 1200 - caption: { text: "The big square must be 100, so b² = 100 − 36 = 64.", say: "The big square must be one hundred. Take away thirty-six: sixty-four." } - click: Make side b longer - click: Make side b longer - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "= 10²" } - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "b = √64 = 8.", say: "So the side is the square root: eight." } - wait: 1200 --- You've got a 4.1 m ladder, and the gutter is 3.9 m up. Ladder safety rules say the foot should go 1 m out from the wall for every 4 m of height ([WorkSafe ACT](https://www.worksafe.act.gov.au/health-and-safety-portal/safety-alerts/ladder-safety), [SafeWork NSW](https://www.safework.nsw.gov.au/hazards-a-z/ladders)), so yours sits about 1 m out. Will it reach the gutter? Have a guess before you read on, and we'll come back to it at the end. The ladder, the wall and the ground make a right-angled triangle. You know the long side, which is the ladder, and the bottom, which is 1 m. What you're after is the height up the wall. (We'll treat the ground as flat.) ## Predict: the ladder ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a height for the 5 m ladder with its foot 3 m out shows whether they subtract the squares or add them as for a hypotenuse." check: type: predict q: "A 5 m ladder leans against a wall. Its foot is 3 m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?" options: ["4 m", "About 5.83 m", "2 m", "8 m"] actual: "4 m. The ladder is the hypotenuse: 5² − 3² = 25 − 9 = 16, so the height is 4 m. 5.83 m adds the squares, which would make the wall taller than the ladder." ``` This is a different ladder from the one at the start, so here's a quick sketch of it. Which side of the triangle is the ladder? ## Run: the height that fits ```step stage: run insight: "Changing b until the hypotenuse is 5 shows that the missing square is the big square minus the known one." try: { playground: board, starter: "tri.yml#run", height: 620 } check: { type: board, text: "The ladder is the hypotenuse, 5 m, and the foot is a = 3 m out. Change the height b until c = 5. Was your prediction right?", when: "c = 5", explain: "b = 4: 9 + 16 = 25. The height's square is 25 − 9 = 16." } ``` Watch the biggest square as b changes: you need it to be 25. ## Investigate: add or subtract? ```step stage: investigate insight: "For a shorter side subtract the squares; Ken adds, and gets a side longer than the hypotenuse. A real problem starts by spotting the right angle and the hypotenuse; students own the working and pick the key reason." tasks: - check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 13 cm and one shorter side 5 cm. How long is the other side, in cm?" steps: - ["$b^2 = 13^2 - 5^2$", "13 is the hypotenuse, so subtract the squares"] - ["$b^2 = 169 - 25 = 144$", "square first, then subtract"] - ["$b = \\sqrt{144} = 12$ cm", "take the square root"] - ["$12 < 13$", "check: the hypotenuse is still the longest"] answer: "12" feedback: - ["13.93", "That adds the squares. The hypotenuse is the longest side: subtract."] - ["8", "That subtracts the sides. Subtract the squares: 169 − 25."] - ["144", "That's the square of the side. Take the square root."] criteria: - "I squared both numbers before taking one from the other." - "I subtracted, because 13 is the hypotenuse." - "My answer is shorter than 13." explain: "13² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144, √144 = 12 cm." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#ken" text: "Ken finds a shorter side. Click the line where his working goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: pyth-add-for-leg explain: "Line 2: 10 cm is the hypotenuse, so subtract: b² = 100 − 36 = 64, b = 8 cm. His 11.66 cm is longer than the hypotenuse, which is impossible." - check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A rectangular screen is 48 cm wide and 36 cm high. How long is its diagonal? Write your steps." steps: - ["The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with sides 48 and 36", "the corners of a rectangle are right angles"] - ["$48^2 + 36^2 = 2304 + 1296 = 3600$", "for the hypotenuse, add the squares"] - ["$\\sqrt{3600} = 60$ cm", "take the square root"] picks: - step: 2 options: ["For the hypotenuse, add the squares", "For the hypotenuse, subtract the squares", "Add the sides: 48 + 36"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Subtract when the hypotenuse is known and a shorter side is missing.", "That is the way round two edges, longer than across."] answer: "60" feedback: - ["84", "That adds the sides. Square them first."] - ["3600", "That is the diagonal's square. Take the square root."] explain: "48² + 36² = 3600, √3600 = 60 cm." ``` ### Add for c, subtract for a side Here are both kinds. ```worked c^2 = 6^2 + 8^2 = 100,\ c = 10 :: Missing the hypotenuse: add the squares. b^2 = 10^2 - 6^2 = 100 - 36 = 64,\ b = 8 :: Missing a shorter side: subtract from the hypotenuse's square. b^2 = 7^2 - 4^2 = 33,\ b = \sqrt{33} \approx 5.74 :: Not a perfect square: between 5 and 6 (25 and 36), about 5.74. 5.74 < 7 :: Check: the hypotenuse must still be the longest. ``` Now try one on paper, set out like the example: hypotenuse 13 cm, one side 5 cm. Look back at the example if you get stuck. ### Find the mistake Read Ken's working. Can a shorter side be longer than the hypotenuse? ### A screen Sketch the screen on paper and mark the hypotenuse, then work it out. ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a side on the board, a ramp with decimals, a side that is not a whole number, a shortcut saving, then the edge case of a shorter side longer than the hypotenuse." try: { playground: board, starter: "tri.yml#six", height: 620 } tasks: - starter: "tri.yml#six" hint: "The big square must be 100. Take away 36." check: { type: board, text: "a = 6. Change b until the hypotenuse is 10.", when: "c = 10", explain: "b = 8: 100 − 36 = 64 = 8²." } - check: type: answer q: "A ramp is 2.6 m long (the sloping side) and goes 2.4 m across the ground. How high does it rise, in m?" answer: "1" feedback: - ["3.54", "That adds the squares, but 2.6 m is the hypotenuse."] - ["0.2", "That subtracts the lengths. Subtract the squares: 6.76 − 5.76."] explain: "2.6² − 2.4² = 6.76 − 5.76 = 1, √1 = 1 m." - check: type: number q: "Hypotenuse 7 cm, one side 4 cm. The other side, in cm, to two decimal places?" answer: 5.74 tolerance: 0.005 explain: "49 − 16 = 33, √33 ≈ 5.74 cm." - check: type: answer q: "Walking round a 30 m by 40 m park is 70 m. How many metres shorter is the path straight across, corner to corner?" answer: "20" feedback: - ["50", "50 m is the path across. How much shorter than 70 m is it?"] explain: "Across: √(900 + 1600) = 50 m, so 70 − 50 = 20 m shorter." - check: type: question q: "Edge case: Jo finds a shorter side of 13 cm in a triangle whose hypotenuse is 12 cm. What does that tell her?" options: ["She made a mistake: a shorter side can't be longer than the hypotenuse", "The triangle is very thin", "She should round to 12 cm"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "No right-angled triangle has a side longer than its hypotenuse.", "Rounding does not fix a method slip: she probably added instead of subtracting."] explain: "The hypotenuse is always the longest side, so she probably added the squares instead of subtracting." ``` ### On the board Each task changes one thing. ### A ramp ### Not a whole number ### A shortcut ### Too long ## Practise: any side ```step stage: practise insight: "A shorter side, a diagonal, a ladder and a review, mixed; adding for a shorter side is the planted slip." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Hypotenuse 25 cm, one side 7 cm. The other side, in cm?" answer: "24" feedback: - ["25.96", "That adds the squares. Subtract: 625 − 49."] explain: "625 − 49 = 576, √576 = 24 cm." - check: type: number q: "A square has sides of 5 cm. How long is its diagonal, in cm, to two decimal places?" answer: 7.07 tolerance: 0.005 explain: "25 + 25 = 50, √50 ≈ 7.07 cm." - check: type: answer q: "A 10 m ladder reaches 8 m up a wall. How far is its foot from the wall, in m?" answer: "6" feedback: - ["12.81", "The ladder is the hypotenuse: subtract."] - ["2", "Subtract the squares, not the lengths."] explain: "100 − 64 = 36, √36 = 6 m." smaller: check: { type: "question", q: "Which length is the hypotenuse here?", options: ["The 10 m ladder", "The 8 m up the wall", "The distance from the wall"], answer: 0, explain: "The right angle is where the wall meets the ground, and the ladder is opposite it. So the ladder is the hypotenuse." } - check: type: answer q: "Review: the sides at the right angle are 9 cm and 12 cm. Hypotenuse, in cm?" answer: "15" feedback: - ["21", "That adds the sides."] explain: "81 + 144 = 225, √225 = 15 cm." ``` ### A shorter side ### A diagonal ### A ladder ### Review: the hypotenuse ## Make: back to the ladder ```step stage: make insight: "Coming back to the opening question: the height up the wall is a shorter side (subtract the squares), and the answer is judged against the gutter and the 1-in-4 rule." tasks: - hint: ["The ladder is the hypotenuse.", "4.1² − 1² = 16.81 − 1."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Your 4.1 m ladder has its foot 1 m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach, in m to two decimal places?" steps: - ["The ladder is the hypotenuse: $c = 4.1$, $a = 1$", "it is opposite the right angle where the wall meets the ground"] - ["$b^2 = 4.1^2 - 1^2 = 16.81 - 1 = 15.81$", "for a shorter side, subtract the squares"] - ["$b = \\sqrt{15.81} \\approx 3.98$ m", "take the square root"] picks: - step: 2 options: ["For a shorter side, subtract the squares", "Add the squares", "Subtract the lengths: 4.1 − 1"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That would make the wall taller than the ladder.", "Subtract the squares, not the lengths."] answer: "3.98" feedback: - ["4.22", "That adds the squares: the wall would be taller than the ladder."] - ["3.1", "That subtracts the lengths, not the squares."] - ["15.81", "That is the square of the height. Take the square root."] explain: "16.81 − 1 = 15.81, √15.81 ≈ 3.98 m." - check: type: question q: "The gutter is 3.9 m up. Set up by the 1-in-4 rule, does the 4.1 m ladder reach it?" options: - "Yes: 3.98 m is above 3.9 m, and 1 m out for about 4 m up fits the rule" - "No: 3.98 m is below 3.9 m" - "Only if the foot is moved closer than 1 m" - "You can't tell without the angle" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Compare 3.98 with 3.90.", "It already reaches. Moving the foot in makes the ladder steeper than the rule allows.", "Pythagoras gives the height from the lengths; no angle is needed."] explain: "It reaches 3.98 m, just above the gutter, and 1 m out for 3.98 m up is close to 1 in 4. In real life you would also want the ladder to reach past the gutter to step off, so a longer ladder is safer." ``` ### How high? Now back to your ladder from the start. On paper, sketch the triangle and mark the hypotenuse before you work anything out. ### Does it reach? **Also used in** - **Wheelchair ramps.** A ramp up to 9 m long can rise at most 1 m for every 14 m along ([Queensland Health, from AS 1428.1](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0029/1477208/Ramps-to-the-house-and-slopes-in-the-garden-slides.pdf)). The sloping surface is the hypotenuse. - **Screen sizes.** A TV or phone is sold by its diagonal, the hypotenuse of the screen. Will it fit the cabinet? - **Square corners.** Builders peg out a 3-4-5 triangle of string to check a corner is a right angle. ```teacher summary: Students use Pythagoras to find the hypotenuse or a shorter side (subtracting the squares), with non-whole answers to two decimal places and a sense check, in contexts such as ladders, screens and ramps (AC9M8M06, node 2). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can find a shorter side of a right-angled triangle. - I can decide whether to add or subtract the squares. - I can solve problems with ladders, screens and ramps, and check my answer makes sense. struggle: Deciding whether to add or subtract. Ask students to point to the hypotenuse and say whether it is the side they know or the side they want, before any calculation. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need the hypotenuse method (previous lesson) and square roots between whole numbers (Between the squares). Pilot (Oct 2026): the lesson opens with a real question (will a ladder set up by the 1-in-4 safety rule reach the gutter?) and Make comes back to it; "Also used in" closes it. The middle of the lesson is unchanged. Tell us whether the opening helps or gets in the way. The one idea: add the squares to find the hypotenuse, subtract them to find a shorter side. The common mistake is adding for a shorter side (Ken's mistake); the check "the hypotenuse is the longest" catches it. running: - "Predict: students who chose 5.83 added; ask whether the wall can be taller than the ladder." - "Run: ask what the big square has to be." - "Investigate: for the screen, share sketches; label the hypotenuse first." - "Modify: for the shortcut, ask what is being compared." - "Make: back to the opening ladder. Ask who thinks it reaches before anyone calculates; then ask what else a real ladder job needs (it should reach past the gutter to step off)." - "Paper: the first Investigate task, the screen and the ladder are worked on paper; the page marks only the answer and then shows a model to compare. Books out for those, and look at the pages, not the screens." stuck: - see: A student adds the squares for a shorter side (Ken's mistake). ask: Is your answer shorter than the hypotenuse? fix: "Subtract: hypotenuse squared minus the known side squared." - see: A student subtracts the lengths, not the squares. ask: What does the theorem say about the squares? fix: Square both, subtract, then root. - see: A student cannot find the triangle in a word problem. ask: Where is the right angle? Which length is opposite it? fix: Sketch it, mark the right angle, label c first. stretch: "A 2 m by 1.5 m door: can a 2.6 m wide board be carried through it, tilted along the diagonal?" support: "Use a decision card: 'Know c? Subtract. Want c? Add.' and keep squares to 20² visible." leads: > Next: Right, acute or obtuse? (node 3): using the theorem backwards to test a triangle. Where it leads: distance between two points, trigonometry (Year 10), and 3D diagonals of boxes. exit: q: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 17 cm and one side 8 cm. Find the other side. a: 289 − 64 = 225, √225 = 15 cm. explain: > Pythagoras finds any side of a right-angled triangle: - the **hypotenuse**: add the squares, $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$; - a **shorter side**: subtract, $b^2 = c^2 - a^2$. Then take the square root (to two decimal places if it is not whole). Check: the hypotenuse must be the longest side. sources: - title: "Ladder safety (WorkSafe ACT): base 1 m out for every 4 m of height" url: https://www.worksafe.act.gov.au/health-and-safety-portal/safety-alerts/ladder-safety checked: 2026-10-22 - title: "Ladders (SafeWork NSW): the same 1:4 rule" url: https://www.safework.nsw.gov.au/hazards-a-z/ladders checked: 2026-10-22 - title: "Ramps to the house and slopes in the garden (Queensland Health): 1:14 for ramps up to 9 m, from AS 1428.1" url: https://www.health.qld.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0029/1477208/Ramps-to-the-house-and-slopes-in-the-garden-slides.pdf checked: 2026-10-22 ```

= 100 + 36 = 136
